summary: Describes a simple IS-IS mechanism that reduces packet loss during transient network conditions, needing no protocol changes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a road changes, cars can get stuck for a moment. This is a trick to avoid that.

questions: when should routers set overload bit
subtitle: Avoiding packet loss when routing protocols converge after a network transient.

tldr.problem: When an IS-IS router reboots or recovers, the network quickly routes packets to it, but the router has not yet learned external routes (via BGP). Packets get dropped while waiting for BGP to synchronize.
tldr.mechanism: A recovering router temporarily sets the Overload bit in its IS-IS advertisement, which tells other routers not to use it as a transit path. It only advertises connections to local networks. Once BGP converges, it clears the bit and becomes available for transit.
tldr.outcome: The router remains reachable for its own networks while protecting packets from being sent to it before it is ready.

facts.label: Typical duration set
facts.value: N seconds after reboot or until BGP converges

today: RFC 3277 is an informational standard describing a proven technique used in production IS-IS networks to prevent transient packet loss during routing convergence. The mechanism is widely implemented by router vendors and deployed by service providers.

sections.title: The Transient Blackhole Problem
sections.content:
In IS-IS networks, when a router that was previously a transit router becomes unavailable (for example, due to a reboot), other routers select alternative paths quickly. The newly selected routers have complete forwarding information bases and can deliver packets correctly.

The problem occurs when the failed router comes back online. Within seconds, it establishes IS-IS neighbor relationships and synchronizes its link-state database. The network immediately recognizes that the optimal path again goes through this router and updates forwarding tables. However, external route information (learned via BGP) has not yet propagated to the recently recovered router. As a result, the router receives packets destined for networks it cannot yet reach and discards them.
sections.eli5: A router comes back online fast and gets traffic sent to it, but it doesn't yet know how to reach the destinations, so it drops the packets.

sections.title: Using the Overload Bit
sections.content:
The solution uses the Overload bit, a flag in IS-IS Link State Packets (LSPs). When a router sets this bit, it tells other routers in the domain to not calculate transit paths through it. The router's own routes to locally connected networks remain advertised and usable.

When a recovering router comes back online, it should immediately flood its new LSP with the Overload bit set, even before synchronizing its link-state database. This signals to all routers in the domain that the recovered router should not be used as a transit router. The recovering router advertises its own loopback address and adjacencies so that other routers can peer with it via BGP, but packets are not routed through it for transit.

After BGP converges and synchronizes external route information, the router generates a new LSP with the Overload bit cleared, and normal routing can resume.
sections.eli5: The router says 'I'm not ready yet' and other routers avoid sending packets through it until it is ready.

sections.title: Deployment and Considerations
sections.content:
This mechanism has been deployed in large IS-IS networks for years and significantly improves overall network availability. It requires no protocol changes and is fully compatible with existing IS-IS specifications.

The trigger for setting the Overload bit is left to the implementer. Common approaches include setting it for N seconds after a reboot or until N BGP prefixes have been learned. In service provider networks where BGP peering uses loopback addresses, the router must advertise its loopback and adjacencies immediately so that BGP neighbors can establish IBGP connections.

One trade-off is that if the Overload bit is set when the router is the only path to reach a downstream network, no packets will reach those networks until the bit is cleared. Additionally, all IS-IS routers in the domain must correctly implement the Overload bit to avoid forwarding loops.
sections.eli5: After rebooting, a router uses the Overload bit until it has learned all the external routes it needs.

sections.title: Comparison with Metric-Based Approaches
sections.content:
An alternative mechanism, similar to OSPF's Stub Router Advertisement (RFC 3137), uses excessively high link metrics instead of the Overload bit. This approach allows transit paths to still be calculated through the router, which can be an advantage if it is the only path available.

However, IS-IS historically provided only 6 bits of space for link metrics and 10 bits for path metrics, giving limited flexibility. Though extensions have been proposed to increase this space, they are not yet widely deployed. The Overload bit approach is simpler and more backward-compatible with existing deployments.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying 'don't use me', a router could say 'I'm very slow right now.' But the simpler approach works better.
